messages.content:
Assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category. Here are worked examples, then the case to code.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: I21

Example 3
Hospital course: A 34-year-old woman presented with fever, rigors, dysuria and right flank tenderness. Urine microscopy showed pyuria and culture grew Escherichia coli. Computed tomography showed a swollen right kidney with no abscess. She improved on intravenous ceftriaxone.
Answer: N10

Example 4
Hospital course: An 81-year-old woman was brought in after a fall at home. She could not weight-bear and the right leg was shortened and externally rotated. A pelvic radiograph showed a displaced subcapital fracture of the right femoral neck. She underwent hemiarthroplasty on day one.
Answer: S72

Example 5
Hospital course: A 19-year-old man presented with 18 hours of periumbilical pain that migrated to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia and a low-grade fever. There was guarding at McBurney's point and the white cell count was 15.2. Laparoscopy confirmed an inflamed, non-perforated appendix.
Answer: K35

Example 6
Hospital course: A 64-year-old woman with a history of oestrogen-receptor-positive breast carcinoma treated five years earlier presented with progressive thoracic back pain. Magnetic resonance imaging showed deposits in T7 and T9 with no cord compression. Biopsy confirmed deposits of breast origin and she received palliative radiotherapy to the spine.
Answer: C79

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary for Case 1:

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 40 years
Gender: Male

Admission Information:
The patient was admitted to the hospital on [REDACTED] with symptoms of general malaise, arthralgia in his extremities, facial cyanosis, and fever (39°C). A medical history of post-traumatic splenectomy was reported.

Hospital Course:
Upon admission, empirical antibiotic therapy was started with ceftriaxone and vancomycin as the patient was diagnosed with secondary sepsis caused by meningitis from Streptococcus pneumoniae. Due to a severe hemodynamic instability, the patient was transferred to the ICU where they exhibited persistent hypotension and an inflammatory state with high levels of CRP and PCT.

The patient underwent continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in hemodiafiltration mode for a total of 68 hours along with Cytosorb cartridge. During this treatment, a general improvement was observed in terms of the patient's hemodynamic and metabolic stability as well as reducing levels of PCT and CRP. The patient's norepinephrine demand decreased significantly throughout the treatment and the patient could be stopped from CRRT after 12 days.

Discharge Information:
After further treatment and observation, the patient was discharged on [REDACTED]. At the time of discharge, the patient was alert, collaborative, tracheotomized, and spontaneously breathing with a recovery of diuresis. The patient was advised to continue with follow-up appointments according to the recommended medical protocols.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Recommendations:
The patient was advised to follow up with medical appointments as per recommended medical protocols.

Answer with the three-character category only.

text:
The case describes pneumococcal meningitis with secondary sepsis in a post-splenectomy patient. In ICD-10-AM, the options are:

- G00 (bacterial meningitis, not elsewhere classified), which includes G00.1 pneumococcal meningitis.
- A40.3 (sepsis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae).

The summary says "secondary sepsis caused by meningitis from Streptococcus pneumoniae", so the meningitis is the underlying infection and the sepsis follows from it. The sepsis would be coded as A40.3 and the meningitis as G00.1. Sequencing is the difficulty, because the Australian coding standards usually put the sepsis first when it is present on admission and treated.

The ICU care with CRRT and Cytosorb was directed at septic shock, which supports choosing sepsis as the principal diagnosis. Against that, the explicit statement that the sepsis was secondary to meningitis points to meningitis as the primary condition. The ICD-10 convention for sepsis with a localized infection is to code the systemic infection first, since A40 and A41 are not dagger/asterisk codes. In ICD-10-AM, G00.1 does not carry an asterisk, so either code could be sequenced first. The Australian Coding Standard on sepsis directs coders to assign the code for the underlying localized infection when the sepsis is due to it, and to add a sepsis code as an additional diagnosis.

Pneumococcal meningitis is classified to G00.1, and the case states that the sepsis resulted from the meningitis, so I will choose G00.

**G00**
